jurisdiction: SC-only. No Georgia law belongs on this post; none was found in the body, Key Takeaways or FAQs. The only Georgia reference is the About the Author line ('across South Carolina and Georgia'), handled below.

verifiedClaims.claim: A Sunset Boulevard car accident is a crash on US-378 — the four-lane, 45-mph arterial cutting through West Columbia and Cayce past Lexington Medical Center.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: US-378 (Sunset Boulevard) runs through West Columbia only: it leaves I-26 at Exit 110 (a single-point urban interchange), passes Lexington Medical Center at 2720 Sunset Blvd, West Columbia 29169, and reaches US-1 (Meeting Street) at the Gervais Street Bridge. The City of Cayce borders West Columbia on the south; Sunset Boulevard does not enter it. Lane count: the City of West Columbia's own plan describes the eastern section as 'a five-lane roadway' (four through lanes plus a center turn lane). Posted speed near the hospital is not published in any primary source found; SCDOT's Columbia-area model codes Sunset Boulevard as a Major Arterial at 35 or 45 mph.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: City of West Columbia, Draft Comprehensive Plan ('bounded on the south by the City of Cayce'); West Columbia Gateway Overlay District Redevelopment Plan (2012) ('a five-lane roadway'); SCDOT Phase 3 TransModeler Settings and Parameters (Sunset Boulevard coded Major Arterial 35/45); lexhealth.com (hospital address)
verifiedClaims.note: Drop 'and Cayce'. Replace 'four-lane, 45-mph' with 'multi-lane' unless the editor keeps the 45 as an unsourced descriptor; the safest wording is 'the multi-lane US-378 arterial through West Columbia past Lexington Medical Center'. The same 'and Cayce' error recurs in the H2 section and in the venue paragraph ('West Columbia or Cayce side of the river').

verifiedClaims.claim: These crashes sit in Lexington County, not Richland, which changes where your case files, who handles your records, and which civil rules govern your claim.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: County is correct: Lexington Medical Center (2720 Sunset Blvd, West Columbia 29169) is in Lexington County, Judicial Circuit 11, courthouse at 205 E. Main Street, Lexington 29072. But the South Carolina Rules of Civil Procedure and the substantive law are identical statewide — venue changes the courthouse, the clerk and the jury pool, not 'which civil rules govern your claim'. Venue in a tort action lies in the county where the defendant resided when the cause of action arose OR where the most substantial part of the act or omission occurred (S.C. Code § 15-7-30(C)), so Lexington is a proper venue for a Sunset Boulevard crash, not the only one.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SC Judicial Branch courthouse directory, Lexington County; S.C. Code § 15-7-30(B)-(D)
verifiedClaims.note: Delete 'and which civil rules govern your claim'. Suggested: 'which changes where your case is filed, which clerk and courthouse handle it, and which county's residents sit on your jury.' Statute text: https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t15c007.php

verifiedClaims.claim: according to the SCDOT 2024 Traffic Count Book, US-378 corridors through the Midlands carry tens of thousands of vehicles per day with peak-period AADT volumes well above the statewide arterial average.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: There is no SCDOT 'Traffic Count Book'; SCDOT publishes annual AADT by count station. 2024 AADT on US-378 in Lexington County: 28,700 between I-26 and Hook Avenue (the Lexington Medical Center segment), 32,500 between Leaphart Road and I-26, and 44,100 between I-20 and Leaphart Road (2023: 31,300 / 33,500 / 44,500). 'Tens of thousands of vehicles per day' is right. 'Peak-period AADT' is a contradiction (AADT is an annual daily average) and SCDOT publishes no 'statewide arterial average' — drop that clause.

verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'SCDOT's 2024 traffic counts put Sunset Boulevard at roughly 28,700 vehicles a day past Lexington Medical Center and up to 44,100 a day between I-20 and Leaphart Road.' verifiedClaims.claim: According to the South Carolina Department of Public Safety's 2023 Traffic Collision Fact Book, Lexington County recorded more than 13,000 reportable traffic crashes in 2023 alone — placing it among the state's top five counties for collision volume.

It ranked 6th of 46 counties for total collisions in both 2023 and 2024 (behind Greenville 16,478; Charleston 15,802; Richland 12,068; Horry 11,103; Spartanburg 10,689). verifiedClaims.claim: Emergency-vehicle right-of-way disputes are common — and legally complicated, because they implicate S.C. Code § 56-5-760.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 56-5-760, 'Operation of authorized emergency vehicles', is on point: (B) lets the driver of an authorized emergency vehicle proceed past red signals after slowing, exceed speed limits and disregard direction-of-movement rules; (C) those privileges apply only while using an audible signal (§ 56-5-4970) and visual signals (§ 56-5-4700); (D) the section 'do[es] not relieve the driver of an authorized emergency vehicle from the duty to drive with due regard for the safety of all persons'. No source counts emergency-vehicle crashes on this corridor, so 'are common' is unsupported.
verifiedClaims.note: Drop 'are common'; keep the statute. Suggested: 'Emergency-vehicle right-of-way disputes are legally complicated, because § 56-5-760 gives ambulance drivers running lights and siren the right to pass red signals and exceed the limit — while still requiring due regard for everyone else's safety.'

verifiedClaims.currentValue: Magistrates have concurrent civil jurisdiction in actions for damages for injury to the person where the damages claimed do not exceed $7,500 (S.C. Code § 22-3-10(2)).
verifiedClaims.note: The editor may state the $7,500 limit.

verifiedClaims.claim: If your crash occurred on the West Columbia or Cayce side of the river, near Lexington Medical Center, your case almost certainly belongs in Lexington County Court of Common Pleas.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Drop 'or Cayce' (Sunset Boulevard is not in Cayce). Under § 15-7-30(C), an action against a resident individual 'must be brought and tried in the county in which the: (1) defendant resides at the time the cause of action arose; or (2) most substantial part of the alleged act or omission giving rise to the cause of action occurred' — so Lexington County is a proper venue for a Sunset Boulevard crash, and the defendant's home county is the alternative.
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'If your crash occurred on the West Columbia side of the river, near Lexington Medical Center, your case is properly filed in Lexington County Court of Common Pleas — the county where the crash happened — unless your lawyer chooses the county where the at-fault driver lives.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Filing in the wrong venue won't necessarily kill your case, but it can cause expensive delay, motions to transfer, and a worse procedural posture going into discovery.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-7-30(B) makes venue 'subject to the power of the court ... to change the place of trial as provided in Section 15-7-100 or as otherwise provided by law'; an improperly venued case is moved, not dismissed.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under S.C. Code § 15-3-530, you generally have three years from the date of injury to file a personal-injury lawsuit in South Carolina.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5) ('any injury to the person or rights of another, not arising on contract')
verifiedClaims.note: Matches the writer-profile table and sibling packs 4729/1653.

verifiedClaims.claim: the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, S.C. Code § 15-78-110, requires filing within two years.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-78-110: barred 'unless an action is commenced within two years after the date the loss was or should have been discovered'; three years if the claimant first filed a verified claim under the Act (which must be received within one year, § 15-78-80). Damages against a governmental entity are capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence (§ 15-78-120(a)).
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate as a rule of thumb. The examples ('a county-employed EMS driver, a city employee, or a state trooper') are all governmental employees within the Act.

verifiedClaims.claim: Hospital-corridor crashes near Lexington Medical Center are exactly the kind of cases where a government defendant can show up unexpectedly.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Lexington County EMS is a county department (Public Safety), running up to twenty ambulances and handling emergency transports only; non-emergency transports are handled by private services. An ambulance leaving the hospital may therefore belong to a governmental entity (Tort Claims Act) or a private company.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: County of Lexington, Emergency Medical Services; EMS FAQs
verifiedClaims.note: Supports the hedge in the body and in faq:4 ('if the ambulance driver works for a government entity').

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina follows a 51% modified-comparative-negligence rule under Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.. If a jury finds you 50% or less at fault, you can still recover — but your damages are reduced by your share of fault. If you are 51% or more at fault, you recover nothing.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991): plaintiff recovers 'if his or her negligence is not greater than that of the defendant', reduced in proportion
verifiedClaims.note: Correctly attributed to Nelson, not § 15-38-15 (which governs apportionment among defendants and is not cited in this post). Verified verbatim in sibling packs 4729/1653/2647/4738. Typo: the body and faq:2 have 'Co..' (double period).

verifiedClaims.claim: According to the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey, more than 90% of South Carolina workers commute by car
verifiedClaims.currentValue: ACS 2023 1-year estimates, table S0801, South Carolina: 84.8% of workers 16+ travelled to work by car, truck or van (76.1% drove alone, 8.7% carpooled); 11.8% worked from home. 'More than 90%' is not supported by the current data.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2023 1-Year Estimates, Subject Table S0801 (Commuting Characteristics by Sex), South Carolina
verifiedClaims.note: The sentence's logic (car commuting share → fault disputes are routine) is a non sequitur; the cleanest fix is to delete the whole sentence. If kept, 'about 85%'.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina's 51% bar is among the more defense-friendly variants in use nationally.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The opposite. Of the two modified-comparative-negligence variants, South Carolina's 'not greater than' rule (a plaintiff exactly 50% at fault still recovers) is the more plaintiff-friendly; the stricter '50% bar' (recovery only if less than 50% at fault) is the defense-friendly one — Georgia uses it, per the writer-profile table.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (1991); profiles/writer-profile.md jurisdiction table (GA 'less than 50%' vs SC 'less than 51%')
verifiedClaims.note: Delete the clause. Do not add the Georgia comparison to this SC-only post.

verifiedClaims.claim: S.C. Code § 38-77-160 permits stacking of UIM coverage across multiple eligible policies. This matters enormously in hospital-corridor crashes, where Lexington Medical Center bills alone can blow through a single at-fault driver's minimum policy limits. If you have multiple vehicles on your policy — or live in a household with multiple insured vehicles — stacking can unlock several layers of coverage you may not know you have.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 38-77-160 is the UIM statute (UIM must be offered; the insured may buy it up to the liability limits), but it limits stacking rather than granting it: an insured with coverage above the basic limits 'is protected only to the extent of the coverage he has on the vehicle involved in the accident', and if none of the insured's vehicles was involved, 'only to the extent of coverage on any one of the vehicles'. Case law confines stacking to Class I insureds (named insured, spouse, resident relatives); Carter v. Standard Fire Insurance Co., 406 S.C. 609, 753 S.E.2d 515 (2013) voided a policy exclusion that conflicted with that statutory right. Minimum liability limits are 25/50/25 (§ 38-77-140).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 38-77-140, 38-77-150, 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire Insurance Co., 406 S.C. 609 (2013)
verifiedClaims.note: Same finding as sibling packs 4729, 1757 and 4738. Suggested: 'South Carolina lets a named insured or resident relative (a Class I insured) stack UIM coverage from other household vehicles and policies, capped at the coverage on the vehicle involved (S.C. Code § 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire, 2013). ... If you or a resident relative insure more than one vehicle, stacking can add layers of coverage you may not know you have.' Carter: https://law.justia.com/cases/south-carolina/supreme-court/2013/27340.html

verifiedClaims.claim: S.C. Code § 56-5-2930 governs DUI in South Carolina.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-2930 (operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs); companion § 56-5-2933 (.08 per se) and § 56-5-2945 (felony DUI)
verifiedClaims.note: Verified in sibling pack 4729.

verifiedClaims.claim: A criminal conviction under this section is persuasive evidence in a civil negligence claim, and can support a dram-shop action against the bar or restaurant that overserved the impaired driver.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No primary source supports 'conviction ... is persuasive evidence' as stated, and the dram-shop link is mis-described. South Carolina has no dram-shop act; a bar or restaurant is liable for knowingly serving an intoxicated patron under §§ 61-4-580(A)(2) and 61-6-2220, treated as negligence per se (Tobias v. Sports Club, 332 S.C. 90 (1998); Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill, 388 S.C. 407 (2010)). For claims arising after January 1, 2026, § 61-2-147 makes the licensee jointly and severally liable for 50% of actual damages when the verdict also runs against a driver charged under §§ 56-5-2930, -2933 or -2945 — the trigger is the charge, not a conviction. The DUI arrest itself generates evidence: § 56-5-2953 requires incident-site and breath-test-site video for every DUI arrest.
verifiedClaims.note: Statutes and cases verified in sibling pack 4729 (2026-09-24). Suggested: 'A DUI charge under this section matters twice in the civil case: the arrest record, breath or blood result and the mandatory dash- and breath-room video (§ 56-5-2953) become evidence, and if a bar or restaurant knowingly served the driver while intoxicated, it can be liable too (§§ 61-4-580, 61-6-2220) — for crashes after January 1, 2026, § 61-2-147 makes it jointly liable for half your actual damages when the driver was charged with DUI.' Hartfield: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1347026/hartfield-v-getaway-lounge-grill-inc/

verifiedClaims.claim: Late-night Sunset Boulevard wrecks frequently involve this fact pattern.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No roadway-level DUI data exists (SCDPS reports DUI collisions by county only).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Traffic Collision Fact Book 2024 Edition

verifiedClaims.claim: S.C. Code § 56-5-760 sets the rules of the road for emergency vehicles. When an ambulance leaves Lexington Medical Center with lights and sirens and is involved in a crash, this statute (and the Tort Claims Act if the responder is government-employed) governs liability — and the analysis is genuinely technical.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 56-5-760 'Operation of authorized emergency vehicles': privileges in (B), lights-and-siren condition in (C), due-regard duty in (D). Lexington County EMS is a county agency; private ambulance services also operate.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-760; S.C. Code § 15-78-110; County of Lexington EMS
verifiedClaims.note: 'sets the rules of the road for emergency vehicles' is a fair gloss; more precisely it sets the privileges and the due-regard duty of the emergency driver. The other drivers' duty to yield is § 56-5-1310, not cited and not needed.

verifiedClaims.claim: S.C. Code § 15-51-10 et seq. governs wrongful-death actions in South Carolina. The claim must be brought by the deceased person's personal representative.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-51-10 creates the action; § 15-51-20: 'Every such action shall be brought by or in the name of the executor or administrator' for the benefit of the spouse and children (or parents, or heirs). The deadline is three years from the death under § 15-3-530(6).
verifiedClaims.note: Optional add: 'within three years of the death (§ 15-3-530(6))'. Matches the writer-profile wrongful-death row.

verifiedClaims.claim: According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's most recent Traffic Safety Facts annual report, more than 6 million police-reported motor-vehicle crashes occur in the United States each year — and the steps a victim takes in the first 72 hours often determine the outcome of any later claim.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: NHTSA, Traffic Safety Facts 2023 (DOT HS 813 738): 6,138,359 police-reported motor vehicle traffic crashes in 2023 (37,654 fatal; 1,697,252 injury; 4,403,453 property-damage-only), up 3.5% from 5,930,697 in 2022. 'More than 6 million' is correct for 2023. The '72 hours' clause is the firm's advice, not NHTSA's; the sentence as built attributes it to NHTSA.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: NHTSA, Traffic Safety Facts 2023: A Compilation of Motor Vehicle Traffic Crash Data (DOT HS 813 738)

verifiedClaims.claim: Soft-tissue injuries and concussions routinely surface 24 to 72 hours later, and a contemporaneous ER record is the most powerful piece of evidence in a soft-tissue case.

verifiedClaims.claim: Get the SCDPS crash report. You can request it through SCDPS or the responding agency.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The collision report (Form TR-310) is issued by the South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles, not SCDPS: request it online or with SCDMV Form FR-50 (rev. 07/2025) at any branch or by mail, $10 per report. SCDPS's own site directs collision-report requests to SCDMV. Municipal police departments can release reports they wrote.

verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Get the collision report. The TR-310 the officer files goes to SCDMV; request it online or with Form FR-50 ($10), or from the responding police department.' Sunset Boulevard is not in Cayce, and a boulevard has no mile-markers. Inside West Columbia the responding agency is West Columbia PD or the Highway Patrol; in the Town of Lexington, Lexington PD.

verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'For a Sunset Boulevard wreck, the responding agency is typically the West Columbia Police Department or the South Carolina Highway Patrol, which investigated most of Lexington County's crashes in 2024.'

The cluster around Lexington Medical Center sits squarely inside Lexington County, so most cases proceed in the Lexington County Court of Common Pleas (11th Judicial Circuit) — not the Richland County 5th Circuit in downtown Columbia.

verifiedClaims.claim: Hurt on Sunset Boulevard (US-378) near Lexington Medical Center? A West Columbia & Lexington County crash guide — venue, SC statutes, what to do.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Lexington Health (2720 Sunset Blvd, West Columbia); SC Judicial Branch (Lexington County)
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as the Article description; accurate.

verifiedClaims.claim: Almost certainly Lexington County. The Sunset Boulevard / Lexington Medical Center corridor sits inside Lexington County, so most personal-injury cases proceed in the Lexington County Court of Common Pleas (11th Judicial Circuit) rather than the Richland County 5th Circuit in downtown Columbia. Federal cases under diversity jurisdiction file in the U.S. District Court, Columbia Division.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Lexington County = Circuit 11; Richland = Fifth Circuit, Columbia; Columbia Division comprises Kershaw, Lee, Lexington, Richland and Sumter (28 U.S.C. § 121(3)). Venue alternative: the defendant's home county (§ 15-7-30(C)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SC Judicial Branch; 28 U.S.C. § 121(3); S.C. Code § 15-7-30
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. 'Almost certainly' is acceptable given 'most ... cases'; optional clause: 'unless your lawyer files where the at-fault driver lives, which South Carolina's venue statute also allows'.

verifiedClaims.claim: In most cases, three years from the date of injury under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. But if your defendant is a state or local government entity — for example, a county-employed EMS driver — the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-110) shortens that to two years. Don't assume you have three years until a lawyer confirms it.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-3-530(5) three years; § 15-78-110 two years from when the loss was or should have been discovered (three if a verified claim was first filed). Lexington County EMS is a county department.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 15-3-530, 15-78-110; County of Lexington EMS
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: You can still recover damages in South Carolina if you were 50% or less at fault, under Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.. Your recovery is reduced by your fault percentage. If a jury finds you 51% or more at fault, however, you recover nothing — which is why aggressive fault-shifting is the defense playbook in nearly every contested claim.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991)
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. Rule and arithmetic correct. Fix the 'Co..' double period. 'nearly every contested claim' is characterization.

verifiedClaims.claim: Look hard at uninsured / underinsured motorist coverage. S.C. Code § 38-77-160 allows stacking of UIM coverage across multiple eligible policies, which can multiply the coverage available to you. Many crash victims have stackable coverage they don't realize they have until a lawyer reviews every household policy.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Stacking is confined to Class I insureds (named insured, spouse, resident relatives) and capped at the coverage on the vehicle involved in the crash (§ 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire, 406 S.C. 609 (2013)). 'Multiply' overstates; UM is mandatory (§ 38-77-150), UIM optional (§ 38-77-160).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 38-77-150, 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire Insurance Co. (2013)
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data — published twice. Suggested: 'Look hard at uninsured / underinsured motorist coverage. Under S.C. Code § 38-77-160, a named insured or resident relative can stack UIM coverage from other household vehicles, up to the coverage on the vehicle involved (Carter v. Standard Fire, 2013). Many crash victims have stackable coverage they don't realize they have until a lawyer reviews every household policy.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Possibly, but it gets technical fast. S.C. Code § 56-5-760 governs emergency-vehicle operations, and if the ambulance driver works for a government entity, the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-110) applies — meaning a two-year filing deadline instead of three, and potential damage caps. Get a lawyer involved before that 2-year window starts running.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Statutes correct: § 56-5-760 (emergency-vehicle operation, due regard); § 15-78-110 (two years from when the loss was or should have been discovered); caps under § 15-78-120(a) are $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence. But the two-year window starts at the crash (when the loss is discovered), so 'before that 2-year window starts running' is wrong — it is already running. Lexington County EMS is a county (governmental) service; private ambulance companies also operate.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 56-5-760, 15-78-110, 15-78-120; County of Lexington EMS
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. Suggested last sentence: 'Get a lawyer involved early — that two-year clock is already running from the day of the crash.' Optional: name the caps ('$300,000 per person under § 15-78-120').

verifiedClaims.claim: You can technically handle it yourself, but most serious-injury claims involve venue questions (Lexington vs. Richland), comparative-fault disputes, UIM stacking analysis, and medical-bill negotiation that benefits enormously from experienced counsel. Roden Law charges no upfront fees and no legal fees unless we win — so the cost of getting evaluated is zero.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Contingency fee, no fees unless we win (writer-profile line 26).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: profiles/writer-profile.md
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. No external factual claim beyond the fee terms.
